newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania announces poll results, unblocks standoff.
newsitem.headline: Albania announces poll results, unblocks standoff.

text.p: Albania's electoral commission announced the final results of parliamentary elections, confirming a big win for President Sali Berisha's Socialist opponents and ending a standoff blocking formation of a new government.
Presidency sources said they expected Berisha to issue a decree on Saturday convening parliament for Monday.

The results of the June 29 poll and two subsequent run-offs gave the Socialists and their coalition allies a total of 117 seats in the 155-seat assembly. The majority of more than two thirds will enable them to carry out their proposals to change the constitution to reduce the power of the president.

Seven of the commission's 17 members had been refusing to approve the results because of a dispute over whether Berisha could be elected as a deputy while holding the office of president. The Socialists wanted guarantees that Berisha would leave office as promised after convening the new parliament.

"In a bid to unblock the crisis, we decided to proclaim final results allowing the president of the republic to convene parliament on Monday as he had proposed," said Fatos Klosi, deputy head of the electoral commission and a representative of the Socialists.
"On the other hand, we agreed to let the commission on mandates have the last say on whether President Sali Berisha should be given the right to become a member of parliament or to remain president."
Berisha reiterated on Thursday that he would resign rather than cohabit with a Socialist government.

The Socialists took 78 seats directly plus another 22 through the proportional system, giving them a total of 100. The Socialists' coalition allies took another 17 seats, and the Democratic Party won 27, including one for Berisha himself.

His government, elected in disputed polls last year, resigned in March at the height of violent protests triggered by the collapse of get-rich-quick pyramid schemes. Tirana, under a 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew, was quiet after the results were announced on Friday night.
International peacekeepers who deployed in April to ensure security for aid deliveries and for the elections started returning home this week.
European Albania envoy Franz Vranitzky warned on Thurday their departure risked leaving a security vacuum in the anarchic country.

Diplomats who have been urging the new government to get to work had expressed concern that there could be no prime minister to attend a donors' meeting in Rome at the end of July to discuss badly-needed aid.

Accusations by the Socialists that Berisha was behind the delay in convening the new parliament followed suggestions by Berisha's supporters that Socialist leader Fatos Nano might be ineligible for the prime minister's post because of a conviction for embezzlement.
His supporters say the charges were politically motivated and he was pardoned by Berisha earlier this year.

Divisions are also reported in Berisha's Democrats over whether the party should rally behind the president or distance itself from him and find a new leader to improve its image, and the party is threatening to boycott the first session of parliament.
